title: The Edict of Milan (313)
hook: Christianity becomes legal, and the persecuted become the favored

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine, and your line was power changes things. Where did you use your bit of power for someone with less? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

A notice goes up on a public wall in Nicomedia, a great city of the eastern empire. It's a letter from two emperors, Constantine, who ruled the west, and Licinius, who was taking hold of the east, who have met at Milan and agreed on how the empire will treat religion. The writer Lactantius copied it out in full. And he notes where it was posted: in the same city where, by his account, an order to tear down churches and burn scriptures had been nailed up some years before. Same city, same kind of wall, opposite message. People who had hidden their books, buried their friends and kept their heads down could walk past and read it. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `A NOTICE ON A WALL IN NICOMEDIA.`

segments.voice: Here's what it actually says, in paraphrase. The emperors grant to Christians, and to all others, the free power to follow whatever religion each person chooses. Hear that again: not Christians instead of everyone else. Christians and everyone else. The letter gives a reason that sounds very Roman: so that whatever divine power there is in heaven may be kindly toward us and toward all who live under our rule. Then it gets practical. The meeting places and property taken from Christians are to be handed back, at once, without payment. And if someone had bought one of those buildings in good faith, they can ask the state for compensation. That's the part that makes it real. Freedom isn't only a sentence; it's a key returned to a door. Now the name. What we call the Edict of Milan reaches us as a letter, and Lactantius gives the copy that Licinius had posted in Nicomedia. The name stuck anyway. Then the turn: the persecuted become the favored. Eusebius keeps letters from the months that follow in which Constantine sends money to clergy in Africa and frees clergy from public duties. That goes past the wall notice. Tomorrow, an emperor calls bishops together. The first letter to Timothy had already asked prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life." Here was that quiet life, arriving all at once. And one more thing, for good and ill. The letter's words were freedom for all. Some readers point out that later, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others. The long story has both. Today, sit with the line as written.
screen: `AN EDICT THAT REACHES US AS A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe slowly. The letter's phrase was Christians and all others. Bring to mind one person near you whose faith is different from yours, or who has none: a neighbor, a coworker, someone in your family. Picture them on an ordinary day, keeping what they keep. A prayer, a fast, a holiday, a quiet Sunday morning with no church in it. Don't argue with it in your head. Just let them be free in the picture. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, the way that old letter named Christians and all others in one breath. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, as they are. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. One of the two emperors whose agreement at Milan gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow their own religion, and handed back what had been taken.

Your line: freedom for all. Today, make room once for someone else's faith, or lack of one: a greeting on their holiday, or a question asked because you really want the answer. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches pray in their services for those in authority and for people who suffer for their faith, and some Christian groups work for religious freedom for people of every faith.

notes: The title carries the date 313 from the index; the spoken script states no date. Confirm the index date.

Lactantius 48: the letter of Constantine and Licinius, posted by Licinius at Nicomedia; grants Christians and all others free choice of religion 'that whatever divinity there is in heaven may be propitious', orders restoration of property without payment, with compensation for buyers. Paraphrased; confirm.
Hook says that in Nicomedia an earlier order to destroy churches and burn scriptures had been posted (Lactantius 12–13). Confirm the link and wording.

Teach says 'in later centuries, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others'. This is a general historical statement not in the cited texts; a Keeper should confirm the framing is fair, or cut it.
Trapdoor: 'not a decree issued at Milan under that title' reflects common scholarly opinion; confirm the wording.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'scholars point out' and the 'build churches' preview (now 'tomorrow, an emperor calls bishops together'), cut the general claim that Christians had prayed for rulers under persecution (1 Timothy now carries it), changed 'read that again' to 'hear that again' for audio, varied the stock 'start with' and 'here's the honest part' lines.

Second editor pass: the unsourced 'in later centuries, when Christians held power' claim is now framed as what 'some readers point out'; the myth item about the name was reworded so it reads cleanly; removed the stale note about bishops traveling on imperial business, which no longer matched the script.

Audit pass: the practice and carry no longer repeat day 762's practice (people suffering for their faith); they now turn to one person of a different faith or none, nearby. Hook: Licinius is 'taking hold of the east' (in early 313 Maximinus Daia still held it). Teach now grounds 'the persecuted become the favored' in Eusebius, Church History 10.6–7 (Constantine's letters sending money to clergy in Africa and exempting clergy from public duties); confirm.
